newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmers press confrontation with government.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmers press confrontation with government.

text.p: Angry Greek farmers showed no sign of backing down in their showdown with the ruling socialists on Monday, causing transport chaos by blockading national road and rail links for a fifth day to back economic demands.

The farmers, choking land transport with a colourful army of thousands of tractors, were massing near the airport at Salonika, Greece's second city and main port in the north, and threatening to close all access roads on Monday, police said.
The farmers were also preparing to cut the highway at Arta, between the northwest city of Ioannina and Athens, which would stop almost all major commercial road transport.
"We see major problems with produce supplies at Athens main central market from tomorrow (Tuesday)," said Dimitris Poulis, president of the giant central market's produce importers.

The farmers began their protest on Thursday by cutting off all main road and rail links between Athens and Salonika. They drove 5,000 tractors on to the motorway and access roads in the Thessaly farm region around the town of Larissa.
They want lower fuel costs, lower value added tax (VAT) on farm equipment, higher price supports -- especially for cotton -- and rescheduling $1.3 billion in debts at state banks.

Bonfires of tyres lit up the night at more than 20 barricades set up by farmers. Despite bitter cold and rain, they were in a festive mood, establishing quarters on the motorways with chairs, tables and plastic tents.
Musicians mingled with the boisterous farmers, singing folk songs to loud cheers and applause. Roadside catering trucks fed demonstrators, many of whom arrived by bus to support the protest.
Banners proclaiming "Don't Give In" hung from overpasses and tractors flew black flags of protest or the blue and white Greek flag.
The revolt is one of the largest demonstrations against a Greek government's economic policies in recent years and seemed to be gaining pace.
Farmers in the fertile Peloponnese on Sunday cut the main national road links between the western port of Patras, whose ferry services link Italy to Greece.

Police reported minor clashes between international truckers coming from Italy and farmers at the Patras barricades. Convoys of trapped commercial trucks, some stretching for more than a kilometre, now line national highways.
Prime Minister Costas Simitis, in his most serious test since winning September elections, remained silent and let senior officials do the talking.

Agriculture Minister Stephanos Tzoumakas, shunning calls by farmers to come to their Larissa headquarters, enflamed passions by charging that the protesters were little more than the political surrogates of opposition parties trying to cause trouble.
An official spokesman said the government had tried to show good faith by sending a team of officials to Larissa, the centre of the rebellion, but he issued a warning as well.
"Both the Greek people and the government cannot and will not be made to feel they are hostages to such actions," spokesman Yannis Nikolaou told a routine news briefing on Monday.
The farmers' protest coincides with a growing number of strikes and demonstrations against the 1997 austerity budget submitted on Friday.
Strikes have been called for this week by prison wardens, teachers, port and tax officials, construction workers and the civil servants union.
